title: Unitary $k$-designs without Hamiltonian quenches
abstract: Unitary designs provide an efficient means of emulating Haar randomness without the requirement of exponential resources. Hamiltonian quench protocols have recently been shown to generate such designs, but achieving this typically requires multiple independent Hamiltonian quenches, even via temporal ensembles. Here, we show that no Hamiltonian quenches are required: a single chaotic Hamiltonian is sufficient to generate approximate unitary $k$-designs. We introduce a two-Pauli-kick (2PK) protocol, where unitary evolution under a fixed Hamiltonian is interspersed with two Pauli operator insertions (kicks). By evaluating the frame potential, we demonstrate that the resulting ensemble converges to the Haar value, indicating the emergence of approximate unitary designs. We verify this protocol for Gaussian random matrix ensembles, the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model, and simplified spin (bosonic) SYK models. Furthermore, our protocol admits a canonical definition of finite-temperature frame potentials and establishes the relation with the partition function. We outline a plausible holographic interpretation of our protocol from the dual gravity picture.
summary: The paper introduces the Two-Pauli-Kick (2PK) protocol as an efficient method to generate approximate unitary k-designs using only a single chaotic Hamiltonian. By analyzing the frame potential across GXE and SYK models, the authors prove that this protocol successfully mimics Haar randomness, thereby circumventing the need for multiple independent quenches in quantum chaos studies.
main_problem: The primary goal is to efficiently generate approximate unitary k-designs, which mimic Haar randomness, without relying on multiple independent Hamiltonian quenches.
main_result: A novel Two-Pauli-Kick (2PK) protocol using a single chaotic Hamiltonian is shown to successfully generate these designs, confirmed by the convergence of the frame potential to the Haar value for various models.
method: The analysis uses the k-th frame potential, $F^{(k)}$, calculated from the temporal ensemble average of unitary evolution interspersed with two random Pauli operator insertions. The method extends to finite temperature via canonical definitions involving partition functions.
model_or_system: The study applies to general many-body quantum systems, tested on benchmark models like Gaussian Random Matrix Ensembles (GXE) and complex chaotic systems such as the Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev (SYK) model in both Majorana and spin formulations.
key_observables: Frame potential $F^{(k)}$, which measures convergence to Haar statistics; finite-temperature generalizations of this potential.
important_parameters: The order of the design ($k$), the inverse temperature ($ eta$), and the time scale limit ($T 	o \infty$ or large Hilbert space dimension $L$).
main_assumptions:
The protocol requires a chaotic Hamiltonian $H$ such that $[P, H] 
eq 0$. The analysis often relies on asymptotic expansions in $1/d$ (Hilbert space dimension).
figures_summary: Figures compare the frame potentials for 1PK vs. 2PK protocols across GXE and SYK models, showing the 2PK protocol approaches the Haar value ($k!$). Other figures illustrate finite-size scaling and thermal potential comparisons.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the problem of generating $k$-designs without multiple quenches. It then details the 2PK protocol and analyzes its success using frame potentials for GXE and SYK models at zero temperature. Subsequent sections generalize this to finite temperatures, establish rigorous lower bounds, and compare different mathematical definitions of the thermal potential.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful theoretical tool (the 2PK protocol) applicable to understanding quantum chaos and scrambling in strongly interacting systems, which is highly relevant for AMO physics studying thermalization dynamics.

It then evolves under the same Hamiltonian for a duration t2, after which the same Pauli kick is applied again, and the evolution continues for a duration t3. The arrow dictates the direction of the operation. The resulting temporal ensemble approaches the Haar ensemble, characterized by the frame potential (3).
